extracted.intended_audience: grant peer reviewers, funding agency staff, and researchers studying peer review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical evaluation of a brief training program to improve reviewers' knowledge of grant review criteria, rating-scale interpretation, scoring accuracy, and inter-rater reliability (using the NIH 9-point scale as the exemplar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the review criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should carefully read and understand the granting agency's criteria so that evaluation scores indicate how well proposals match the agency’s criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The training emphasized that agencies depend on reviewers for accurate information and asked reviewers to carefully read the grant review criteria; participants receiving training spent more time reading the criteria (M = 6.1 min) than controls (M = 4.2 min). The paper suggests clearly defining tasks and showing relevance so reviewers know what is expected and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the rating scale and meaning of each value
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must understand the rating scale (example: NIH 9-point scale) and the meaning of each numerical value (e.g., 1 = exceptional, 5 = good with at least one moderate weakness, 9 = poor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training discussed the meaning of each scale score in detail and used examples (e.g., a score of 2 = outstanding with negligible weaknesses; 4 = very good with numerous minor weaknesses; 5 = good with at least one moderate weakness; 7 = fair with at least one major weakness). Reverse coding (lower numbers = better) was emphasized to reduce selection errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to assign scores that reflect how well the proposal matches criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation scores should indicate how well the proposal matches the agency’s criteria rather than reflect reviewers' idiosyncratic grading habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training presented proposal summaries, asked participants to assign numerical ratings, and provided the correct answers to improve mapping of observed strengths/weaknesses to the appropriate score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding and application of definitions for minor, moderate, and major weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should apply consistent definitions for degrees of weakness (minor/moderate/major) when assigning scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The video discussed NIH definitions (e.g., minor: does not substantially lessen the project’s potential) and how these degrees of weakness map onto rating-scale values; applying these definitions helps standardize score assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of anchoring bias (against academic grading habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should avoid inappropriately applying academic grading models (e.g., collapsing low-percentile differences into a single 'fail' grade) which can anchor scores and restrict range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper describes an analogy: academics may treat 50th percentile as 'fail' and then map to mid-scale on grant scores, inflating scores. Training explicitly addressed anchoring bias and contrast between academic grades and grant rating scales to reduce score inflation and restriction-of-range problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the full range and correct direction of the scale (reverse coding awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be aware if a scale is reverse-coded (lower = better) and should use the full scale range appropriately rather than clustering scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The training discussed reverse coding and importance of each value to prevent errors associated with misinterpreting scale direction; examples contrasted academic midpoint interpretations with NIH scale meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of consequences of inaccurate or inappropriate scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should understand that small differences in scores can influence funding decisions and that scores have real consequences for proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The training used an example showing how minor differences in overall evaluation scores influence whether a proposal falls into a high acceptable range and thus the likelihood of funding; this was used to motivate careful, accurate scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring accuracy (matching the true rating-scale values)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric of quality is the percentage of assigned scores that match the correct rating-scale values (i.e., accuracy of selecting the intended numeric value given the descriptor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, trained participants had higher scoring accuracy (74%) than untrained (35%). Accuracy was assessed by asking participants to map verbal proposal descriptions (taken from NIH descriptors) to the correct numeric score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (consistency among reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review processes should produce consistent ratings among reviewers; inter-rater reliability can be quantified (e.g., intra-class correlations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend ICCs and used a two-way random effects model for agreement on single measures (ICC(2,k)/Model B). Training increased ICC (r_icc = 0.89 trained vs. 0.61 untrained). Choice of ICC model matters; ICCs tend to perform better than some alternatives for multi-rater situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should be calibrated—i.e., aligned in their interpretation and application of the scale and criteria—so that group-level statistics (means) are meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewers are not well calibrated, the reliability and validity of grant reviews may be compromised. The paper treats calibration as a training objective and motivation for brief interventions administered just before review to minimize recall issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer effort/engagement (time and attention spent on criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review quality depends on reviewer effort—specifically time spent reading and attending to the review criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training increased time spent reading criteria. The questionnaire asked whether participants read the criteria and how much time they spent; this behavioral measure correlated with improved accuracy and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer familiarity and experience as a relevant factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers' prior extramural review experience and familiarity with rating scales influence baseline knowledge and behavior; novices may benefit differently from training than experienced reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants self-reported experience; novices (no extramural experience) and experienced (average 19 panels) were compared. The study found training improved both groups, and experienced reviewers may overestimate their knowledge of scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation of other extraneous biases and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Review processes should seek to identify and reduce other sources of noise (bias, mismatch between reviewer expertise and proposal topic, motivation, emotional factors) that can decrease scoring precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists sources of noise (understanding of criteria, familiarity with process, topical match, bias, extraneous factors) and notes that the training targeted only scale interpretation; further work is needed to address other biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate statistical choice for measuring reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating inter-rater reliability, choose a metric suited to the study design and number of raters—ICC models are recommended for more than two raters and when seeking agreement rather than just consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors justify using ICC with two-way estimation for agreement on single values (ICC(2,k)/Model B) and note that Mueller & Buttner and Shrout & Fleiss provide guidance; selection of method is essential for interpretable estimates across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and format of reviewer training (brief, just-in-time interventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver brief, focused training (e.g., an 11-minute video) just prior to reviewing to improve recall and calibration on rating-scale usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study used an 11-minute professional video that emphasized five key issues; authors suggest such brief interventions can be effective and should be administered immediately prior to reviewing to minimize recall decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating rating scales appropriately when aggregating scores (interval vs ordinal assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding agencies should consider whether rating scales are being interpreted at interval level (equal distances between values) because aggregation (means) assumes interval properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper warns that substantial deviations from interval-level interpretations across reviewers make means less informative; improving inter-rater reliability and validity through training supports meaningful aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of score inflation due to benevolence or unfamiliarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not inflate scores out of hesitancy to assign negative ratings due to unfamiliarity with content or desire to give benefit of the doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note this as an observed anti-pattern: untrained reviewers tended to assign more favorable scores for lower-quality proposals. Training aimed to reduce this tendency by clarifying scale meanings and consequences.
